hints: Differentiate the relation implicitly, treating $y$ as a function of $x$.
The restriction on $y$ makes $\cos y$ positive, so replace it by $\sqrt{1-\tan^2x}$.
Rewrite the square root using $\cos2x=\cos^2x-\sin^2x$ and simplify the powers of $\cos x$.
walkthrough:
Start with the relation between $x$ and $y$:
$$\sin y = \tan x$$

Differentiate both sides implicitly with respect to $x$:
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(\sin y) = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(\tan x)$$
$$\cos y\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \sec^2 x$$

Express $\cos y$ in terms of $x$ using the Pythagorean identity $\cos^2 y + \sin^2 y = 1$:
$$\cos y = \sqrt{1 - \sin^2 y}$$
(The positive square root is chosen because $-\frac{1}{2}\pi < y < \frac{1}{2}\pi$, where $\cos y > 0$.)

Substitute $\sin y = \tan x$ into the square root:
$$\cos y = \sqrt{1 - \tan^2 x}$$

Substitute this expression for $\cos y$ into the derivative:
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{1}{\cos^2 x\sqrt{1 - \tan^2 x}}$$

Group one factor of $\cos x$ with the square root and bring it inside:
$$\cos^2 x\sqrt{1 - \tan^2 x} = \cos x \left(\cos x\sqrt{1 - \tan^2 x}\right) = \cos x\sqrt{\cos^2 x(1 - \tan^2 x)}$$

Expand inside the square root using $\tan x = \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$:
$$\cos^2 x(1 - \tan^2 x) = \cos^2 x - \cos^2 x\left(\dfrac{\sin^2 x}{\cos^2 x}\right) = \cos^2 x - \sin^2 x$$

Apply the double angle identity $\cos 2x = \cos^2 x - \sin^2 x$:
$$\cos^2 x - \sin^2 x = \cos 2x$$

Substitute back to obtain the final expression:
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{1}{\cos x\sqrt{\cos 2x}}$$
This completes the proof as required.
